en: Thus have I heard— Dīgha Nikāya 19, the Mahāgovinda Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.

Then Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabbas, at the end of the night, having illuminated the entire Vulture Peak Mountain with his surpassing beauty, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [stood before] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Pañcasikha the son of the gandhabbas said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, that which I have heard and received directly from the presence of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, I shall report that to the Blessed One.
"Report it to me, Pañcasikha," the Blessed One said.
1. The Assembly Hall of the Gods:

"Venerable sir, in former days, even further back, on the fifteenth-day Uposatha, on the full-moon night of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, all the Tāvatiṃsa gods would sit together and assemble in the Sudhamma assembly hall."
A great divine assembly was seated all around, and the four Great Kings were seated in the four directions:
in the eastern direction, the Great King Dhatarattha sat facing west, with the gods in front of him;
in the southern direction, the Great King Virulhaka sat facing north, with the gods in front of him.
In the western direction, the Great King Virūpakkha sat facing the east, with the gods in attendance before him;
in the northern direction, the Great King Vessavaṇa sat facing the south, with the gods in attendance before him.
When, venerable sir, all the Tāvatiṃsa gods had assembled and were seated in the Sudhamma assembly hall...
A great divine assembly had gathered and was seated all around,
and the Four Great Kings were seated in the four directions— this was their seat;
only afterwards did our own seats come to be.
"Venerable sir, those gods who have recently been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa host after practicing the holy life under the Blessed One outshine the other gods in both beauty and glory.
Because of this, venerable sir, the Tāvatiṃsa gods are uplifted, joyful, and filled with rapture and happiness, thinking:
'Ah, indeed, the divine hosts are being replenished, while the asura hosts are diminishing!'"
Then, Bhante, Sakka, lord of the devas, perceiving the confidence of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, rejoiced with these verses:
"Truly, the devas rejoice,
the Tāvatiṃsas together with their leader!"
Honoring the Tathāgata and the excellent nature of the Dhamma,
and beholding the newly arisen devas, they dwell with joyful hearts.
Endowed with beauty and renown,
having practiced the holy life under the Sugata,
they have now come here.
They outshine others in beauty, fame, and long life—
these disciples of the one of vast wisdom.
Having attained distinction here,
seeing this, the Tāvatiṃsa gods together with their lord rejoice.
"Revering the Tathāgata and the excellence of the Dhamma"— with these words,
venerable sir, the gods of the Thirty-three became even more uplifted, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness.
“Indeed, sirs, the divine hosts are increasing, while the asura hosts are diminishing.

Then, venerable sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, perceiving the confidence of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas: [2. The Eightfold Description of Things as They Really Are]... (The eight points follow) ... Then, venerable sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, having understood the confidence of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
“‘Would you like to hear, sirs, eight true praises of that Blessed One? ‘We would like to hear them, sir,’ they replied.
Then, Bhante, Sakka, lord of the devas, recited these eight true praises of the Blessed One to the Tāvatiṃsa devas:”
"What do you think, worthy gods of the Thirty-three?
To what extent has that Blessed One practiced for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans?
To such an extent has he practiced for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness [of gods and humans]."
Among gods and humans, we do not perceive any teacher endowed with this quality in the past, nor indeed at present, other than that Blessed One.
Furthermore, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by that Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
In this way, we do not see any teacher endowed with these qualities as one who teaches the Dhamma that leads onward, either in the past or at present, other than that Blessed One.
That Blessed One has well proclaimed: "This is wholesome"; he has well proclaimed: "This is unwholesome. He has well proclaimed: "This is blameworthy, this is blameless;
this is to be cultivated, this is not to be cultivated; this is inferior, this is sublime; this is dark, this is bright, with their counterparts."

In this way, we do not see, either in the past or now, any teacher endowed with this factor who is an expounder of phenomena that are wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, to be cultivated and not to be cultivated,
inferior and superior, and dark and bright counterparts— except for that Blessed One.
Moreover, the path leading to Nibbāna has been well-expounded by that Blessed One for his disciples; Nibbāna and the path are in harmony.

Just as the waters of the Ganges flow together and meet with the waters of the Yamunā, even so the path leading to Nibbāna has been well-expounded by that Blessed One for his disciples; Nibbāna and the path are in harmony.
In this way, we perceive no teacher endowed with these qualities—who proclaims the path leading to Nibbāna—either in the past or at present, other than that Blessed One.

Indeed, the gains of that Blessed One have been achieved, his fame has been established, such that even the khattiyas dwell as if filled with affection for him; moreover, that Blessed One consumes food free from intoxication.
In this way, we do not see any teacher, either in the past or at present, other than that Blessed One, who partakes of food free from intoxication and endowed with this quality.
Moreover, that Blessed One has found companions among those in training, those practicing the path, and those whose taints are destroyed and who have lived the holy life;
yet, having sent them away, he dwells devoted to solitude.
In this way, we do not see, either in the past or now, any teacher endowed with these qualities who is devoted to delighting in solitude, except for that Blessed One.
Furthermore, that Blessed One acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts; thus he is one who acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts.
In this way, we do not see, either in the past or now, any teacher endowed with these qualities who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, except for that Blessed One.
‘Furthermore, that Blessed One has crossed over doubt, is free from perplexity, has reached the end of his intention,

and has fulfilled his resolve regarding the primary goal of the holy life. We do not see any teacher, past or present, who possesses these qualities— having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having reached the end of his intention,
and having fulfilled his resolve regarding the primary goal of the holy life— with the exception of that Blessed One.’”
"Venerable sir, these eight true praises of the Blessed One Sakka, lord of the devas, did Sakka recite for the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Because they heard these eight true praises of the Blessed One, the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven became even more uplifted, joyful, glad, and filled with rapture and happiness.
Thereupon, venerable sir, some of the devas said this:"
"O friends, oh that four perfectly enlightened Buddhas might arise in the world and teach the Dharma, just as the Blessed One does!
That would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
Some deities spoke thus:
“Let alone, sirs, four perfectly enlightened Buddhas; oh, sirs, may three perfectly enlightened Buddhas arise in the world and teach the Dhamma just as the Blessed One does!
That would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
Some gods spoke thus.
"Let alone, sirs, three perfectly enlightened Buddhas; oh, sirs, may two perfectly enlightened Buddhas arise in the world and teach the Dhamma just as the Blessed One does!
That would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
When this was said, Bhante, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
"It is impossible, gentlemen, it cannot happen, that two Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system; such a thing is not possible.
Oh, gentlemen, may that Blessed One remain free from illness and affliction for a long, long time!
That would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans."
Then, venerable sir, whatever matter it was for which the Tāvatiṃsa devas had gathered and assembled in the Sudhamma hall,
after considering that matter and deliberating upon that matter, those four Great Kings would also speak regarding that matter.
Even after these words of instruction were spoken, those four Great Kings remained in their respective seats, neither moving nor departing from that place.
Having heard the speech of the kings,
they accepted the instruction.
"With serene minds,
they stood together on their seats. Then,
venerable sir, a sublime light arose from the northern direction, and a radiance appeared that surpassed even the splendor of the gods.
Then, Bhante, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
“Friends, as these signs are seen—exalted light arises, radiance becomes manifest—Brahmā will appear.
For this is the preliminary sign for the appearance of Brahmā: namely, that light arises and radiance becomes manifest.”
Just as these signs are seen,
Brahmā will appear;
for this is the sign of Brahmā.
“The radiance is vast and great.
3. The Discourse on Sanaṅkumāra:
Then, venerable sir, the Tāvatiṃsa devas sat down each in their own seats, [thinking]: “The Radiance is vast and great.”
‘We shall know this radiance; we shall go only after we have realized what its result will be.
The four Great Kings also sat down in their respective seats, thinking:
‘We shall know this radiance; we shall go only after we have realized what its result will be.’
Having heard this, the Tāvatiṃsa devas became one-pointed in mind, thinking:
“We shall know this radiance; we shall go there only after having realized what its result will be.
Venerable sir, when Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appears to the Tāvatiṃsa devas, he appears having manifested a gross physical form.
"But, Bhante, that natural form of Brahmā is unattainable for the eyes of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
When, Bhante, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appears before the Tāvatiṃsa devas, he outshines the other devas both in beauty and in glory.
Just as, Bhante, that form and appearance outshines a human form."
In the same way, venerable sir, when Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appears before the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he outshines the other gods both in beauty and in glory.
When, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appears before the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, not a single god in that assembly bows down to him, rises up for him, or invites him to a seat.
Instead, they all sit cross-legged in silence with their hands joined in reverential salutation:
‘Whichever god, O Lord, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra desires to sit upon his couch, upon that god’s couch he shall sit.
And whichever god, O Lord, upon whose couch Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra sits, that god obtains a sublime attainment of inspiration, that god obtains a sublime attainment of joy.
Just as, O Lord, a consecrated kṣatriya king who has been newly anointed to sovereignty obtains a sublime attainment of inspiration, obtains a sublime attainment of joy; so too does that god.
"In the same way, Bhante, whichever deity Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra sits upon his throne gains a sublime attainment of rapture; that deity gains a sublime attainment of joy.
Then, Bhante, having perceived the confidence of the Tāvatiṃsa deities, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra vanished and rejoiced with these verses:
‘Truly, the gods rejoice!...’"
The Thirty-three gods, together with Indra,
paid homage to the Tathāgata and to the excellence of the Dhamma.
Beholding the new god,
the one of beautiful form and great renown,
[they practice] the holy life under the Sugata.
Having practiced here and come back,
they outshine others in beauty, fame, and long life.
The disciples of the one of vast wisdom have attained distinction here;
seeing this, they rejoice.
The Thirty-three gods together with Indra,
paying homage to the Tathāgata and to the excellence of the Dhamma.
"Venerable sir, this was the meaning spoken by Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra.
Venerable sir, when Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra spoke, his voice possessed eight qualities: it was distinct, intelligible, sweet, pleasant to hear, clear, far-reaching, deep, and resonant.
Moreover, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra made himself understood by his voice according to the assembly, yet his sound did not issue beyond that assembly."
"Venerable sir, one who possesses such a voice endowed with these eight factors is called 'one with the Brahma-voice.
Then, venerable sir, the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven said this to the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra:
'Excellent, Great Brahmā! It is precisely by understanding this that we rejoice.'"
‘And there are eight true praises of that Blessed One spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas;
and it is by reflecting upon these that we rejoice.
4. The Eight True Praises.
Then, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
“It would be well, lord of the devas, if we too might hear eight true praises of that Blessed One.
“Very well, Great Brahmā,” replied Sakka, lord of the devas, and he recited eight true praises of the Blessed One to Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra.
‘What do you think, venerable Mahābrahmā?

To what extent has that Blessed One practiced for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans?
To that same extent has he practiced for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness [of gods and humans].’
In this respect, among gods and humans, we do not see any teacher endowed with such qualities in the past, nor do we see one now, other than that Blessed One.
Furthermore, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by that Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
In this way, we do not see any teacher endowed with these qualities as a proclaimer of the Dhamma that leads onward, either in the past or now, other than that Blessed One.
Indeed, by that Blessed One it has been well-proclaimed: "This is wholesome," and "This is unwholesome";
"This is blameworthy, this is blameless; this is to be cultivated, this is not to be cultivated; this is inferior, this is..."
"Exalted; this is the counterpart of the dark and the bright"—thus it is well-proclaimed.

Such is the one who makes known the states that are wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, inferior and exalted, and the counterparts of the dark and the bright.
In this respect, we do not see any teacher endowed with such qualities, neither in the past nor now, other than that Blessed One.
Moreover, the path leading to Nibbāna well-expounded by that Blessed One converges with Nibbāna and the path itself.
Just as the waters of the Ganges converge and meet with the waters of the Yamunā,
even so the path leading to Nibbāna well-expounded by that Blessed One for his disciples converges with Nibbāna and the path itself.
In this way, we do not perceive any teacher, even in the past, nor indeed now, who possesses these qualities as the proclaimer of the path leading to Nibbāna, other than that Blessed One.
Furthermore, the gains of that Blessed One have been accomplished, his fame has been established, and even the khattiyas dwell as if filled with affection for him.
Moreover, that Blessed One consumes food free from intoxication.
We do not see any teacher, either in the past or at present, other than that Blessed One, who is endowed with this quality of taking food free from intoxication.

Furthermore, having gained companions among those in training, those practicing the path, and those whose taints are destroyed and who have lived the holy life, the Blessed One dwells devoted to solitude after having sent them away.
In this way, we do not see any teacher in the past, nor indeed at present, who is devoted to delighting in solitude and endowed with this quality, other than that Blessed One.
For that Blessed One acts as he speaks, and speaks as he acts;
thus he is one who acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts.
In this way, we do not see, either in the past or now, a teacher endowed with these qualities who has practiced in accordance with the Dhamma, except for that Blessed One.
Furthermore, that Blessed One has crossed over doubt, is free from perplexity, has reached the end of his intention, and has attained the primary goal of the holy life.
Thus he has crossed over doubt, is free from perplexity, has reached the end of his intention, and has attained the primary goal of the holy life.
“‘We do not see a teacher endowed with even this one factor in the past, nor do we see one now in the present, other than that Blessed One.
Thus, Bhante, Sakka, lord of the devas, recited these eight true praises of the Blessed Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra.
And because he heard these eight true praises of the Blessed One, Bhante, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra was uplifted, gladdened, and filled with joy and happiness.”
Then, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra manifested a gross physical form and appeared before the Tāvatiṃsa devas in the guise of a youth named Pañcasikha.
Rising up into the air, he sat cross-legged in the sky, in the firmament.
Just as, venerable sir, a strong man might sit cross-legged on a well-spread couch or on a level patch of ground; so did he sit cross-legged in the sky.
In the same way, Bhante, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, having risen into the air and sat cross-legged in the sky, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
“What do you think, worthy Tāvatiṃsa devas? For how long has that Blessed One been possessed of great wisdom?”
Once upon a time, sir, there was a king named Disampati.
King Disampati had a brahmin chaplain named Govinda,
and King Disampati had a son, a prince named Reṇu.
The brahmin Govinda had a son, a young brahmin student named Jotipāla.
Thus, Prince Reṇu and the young brahmin student Jotipāla, along with six other kṣatriyas, were these eight companions.
Then, after some days and nights had passed, the brahmin Govinda died.
When the brahmin Govinda had passed away, King Disampati lamented:

"Alas, friends! At the very time when we had entrusted all our duties to the brahmin Govinda and were enjoying ourselves, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, at that very time the brahmin Govinda has passed away."
When this was said, Lord, Prince Reṇu spoke thus to King Disampati:
“Do not, O Lord, lament excessively over the death of the brahmin Govinda.
There is, O Lord, a young brahmin student named Jotipāla, the son of the brahmin Govinda, who is even wiser than his father and more capable of discerning what is beneficial.”
“Even those matters his father instructed him in were [already] contained within the instruction of the young brahmin Jotipāla.
“Is it so, prince?
“It is so, Your Majesty.”
6. The Story of Mahāgovinda.
Then, sirs, King Disampati addressed a certain man:
“Come, good man, go to where the young Brahmin Jotipāla is; having approached him, speak thus to the young Brahmin Jotipāla:”
“May it be well with the venerable Jotipāla! King Disampati summons the young brahmin Jotipāla; King Disampati desires to see the venerable young brahmin Jotipāla.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” that man replied to King Disampati, and having done so, he approached the young brahmin Jotipāla. Having approached him, he said this to the young brahmin Jotipāla:
“May it be well with the venerable Jotipāla! King Disampati summons the young man Jotipāla; King Disampati desires to see the young man Jotipāla.
“Very well, sir,” Jotipāla the young man replied to that man, and he approached King Disampati. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with King Disampati.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Master, King Disampati said this to the young man Jotipāla:
“May the venerable Jotipāla instruct us; may the venerable Jotipāla not refuse our instruction.
I shall establish you in your father’s position and anoint you as a Govinda.”
“Yes, sir,” the young brahmin Jotipāla replied to King Disampati.
Then, sir, King Disampati anointed the young brahmin Jotipāla as the Govinda and established him in his father’s position.

Once anointed and established in his father’s position as the Govinda, Jotipāla administered those affairs that his father had administered, and he also administered those affairs that his father had not administered.

Whatever tasks his father had successfully accomplished, he too successfully accomplished those same tasks; and whatever tasks his father had not successfully accomplished, he too successfully accomplished those same tasks.
People said of him:
"The Brahmin is indeed a Govinda! The Brahmin is indeed a Mahāgovinda!"
"In this way, sirs, the designation ‘Mahāgovinda’ arose for the young brahmin Jotipāla.
6.1. The Division of the Kingdom Then, sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those six kshatriyas; having approached them, he said this to the six kshatriyas:
“Sirs, King Disampati is old, aged, advanced in years, come to the end of his life’s span, and has reached the final stage of existence. Who indeed, sirs, knows what life may bring?
It is quite possible that when King Disampati has passed away, the royal ministers will anoint Prince Reṇu in the kingdom.
Come, sirs, approach Prince Reṇu; having approached him, speak thus to Prince Reṇu:”
“We are indeed dear, beloved, and pleasing companions to you, sir Reṇu; whatever happiness you have, that is our happiness, and whatever suffering you have, that is our suffering.
Sir, King Diśampati is old, aged, advanced in years, come to the end of his life’s span, and has reached the final stage of existence; who, sir, knows what life holds?
It is quite possible, however, that once King Diśampati has passed away, the royal officials will anoint you, sir Reṇu, in the kingdom.”
“If, sir Reṇu, you should obtain the kingdom, please share the kingdom with us.
“Very well, sirs,” those six kṣatriyas replied to the brahmin Mahāgovinda. Having assented, they approached Prince Reṇu and, having approached him, said this to Prince Reṇu:
“We are indeed your companions, dear to you, pleasing to you, and not disagreeable to you.”
Whatever happiness you have, that is our happiness; whatever suffering you have, that is our suffering.
Sir, King Disampati is aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of his life’s span, and has reached old age; who indeed, sir, knows what life holds?
It is possible, however, that when King Disampati has passed away, the royal officials will anoint you, Reṇu, in the kingship.
“If, sir Reṇu, you should obtain the kingdom, would you share the kingdom with us?
“Who else indeed, sirs, could there be in my realm who might be as happy as you?
If I, sirs, should obtain the kingdom, I will share the kingdom with you.”
Then, sir, with the passing of days and nights, King Disampati died.
When King Disampati had passed away, the royal officials anointed Prince Reṇu in the kingship.
Having been anointed to the kingship, Reṇu, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, enjoyed himself.
Then, sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those six kshatriyas; having approached them, he said this to the six kshatriyas:
"Sirs, King Disampati has passed away.
Reṇu has been consecrated to the kingship and, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, he is enjoying himself."
"But who indeed, sirs, knows that sensual pleasures are intoxicating?
Come, gentlemen, approach King Reṇu and, having approached him, say this to King Reṇu:
'Sire, King Disampati has passed away and you, sir, have been anointed to the kingship; do you remember that promise?'"
“Yes, sir,” those six kṣatriyas replied to the brahmin Mahāgovinda. They approached King Reṇu and, having approached him, said this to King Reṇu:
“Sir, King Diśampati has passed away and you, sir, have been anointed to the kingship. Do you remember that promise?
“I do remember that promise, sirs.”
“Who indeed, sir, is capable of dividing this great earth—long from north to south and broad from east to west—into seven equal and well-proportioned parts?
“Who indeed, sir, is capable of this, other than the brahmin Mahāgovinda?
Then, sir, King Reṇu addressed a certain man:
“Come, good man, go to where the brahmin Mahāgovinda is; having approached him, say this to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
‘Venerable sir, King Reṇu summons you.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” that man replied to King Reṇu, and he went to where the brahmin Mahāgovinda was. Having approached him, he said this to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
“Venerable sir, King Reṇu summons you.
“Very well, sir,” the brahmin Mahāgovinda replied to that man. He then approached King Reṇu and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, King Reṇu said this to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
“Come, Master Govinda, divide this great earth—long from north to south and shaped like the front of a cart—from east to west into seven equal and well-proportioned parts.

“Very well, sir,” the brahmin Mahāgovinda replied to King Reṇu, and he divided this great earth—long from north to south and shaped like the front of a cart—into seven equal and well-proportioned parts.
He established all the divisions in the shape of a cart’s front.
There, indeed, lay the central kingdom of King Reṇu.
Dantapura was the capital of the Kaliṅgas,
and Potana that of the Assakas.
Mahesayaṃ of the Avantīs,
Roruka of the Sovīras,
and Mithilā of the Videhas.
Campā was established among the Aṅgas;
and Bārāṇasī among the Kāsīs— these were established by Govinda.
Then, sirs, those six kṣatriyas were delighted with their respective gains, their intentions fulfilled, thinking:
"Truly, that which we had wished for, that which we desired, that which was intended, that which we longed for—that has been obtained by us.
[These were] Sattabhū and Brahmadatta...
Vessabhū, Bharata,
Reṇu, and two Dhataraṭṭhas—
these were the seven Bhāradvājas at that time.
The first recitation section is finished.
6.2. The Rise of Renown.
Then, sirs, those six kṣatriyas approached the brahmin Mahāgovinda; having approached, they said this to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
"Just as Master Govinda is a friend, dear, pleasing, and agreeable to King Reṇu, even so is Master Govinda a friend, dear, pleasing, and agreeable to us as well. May Master Govinda instruct us;
may Master Govinda not refuse to instruct us."
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Mahāgovinda replied to those six kshatriyas.
Then, sir, the brahmin Mahāgovinda governed the seven anointed kshatriya kings and taught the mantras to seven wealthy brahmins and seven hundred bath-graduates.
Then, sir, after some time, this fair report concerning the brahmin Mahāgovinda spread abroad:
“‘The brahmin Mahāgovinda has seen Brahmā; the brahmin Mahāgovinda has conversed with, spoken to, and deliberated with Brahmā—this is witnessed by him.
Then, sir, this thought occurred to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
‘Indeed, such a fine reputation of mine has spread abroad:’”
‘The brahmin Mahāgovinda has seen Brahmā; the brahmin Mahāgovinda converses with Brahmā, chats with Brahmā, and deliberates with Brahmā.
Yet I have not seen Brahmā, nor do I converse with Brahmā, nor chat with Brahmā, nor deliberate with Brahmā.
However, I have heard this from aged and venerable brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:
‘Whoever retreats into seclusion for the four months of the rains and meditates on the meditation of compassion sees Brahmā, converses with Brahmā, speaks with Brahmā, and deliberates with Brahmā.
‘What if I were to retreat into seclusion for the four months of the rains and meditate on the meditation of compassion?
Then, sir, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached King Reṇu; having approached, he said this to King Reṇu:
“Sir, such a fine reputation has spread about me:
‘The brahmin Mahāgovinda can see Brahmā; the brahmin Mahāgovinda converses with Brahmā, chats with Brahmā, and consults with Brahmā.
Yet, sir, I do not see Brahmā, nor do I converse with Brahmā, nor chat with Brahmā, nor consult with Brahmā.”
Moreover, I have heard this from aged and elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:

"Whoever retreats into seclusion for the four months of the rainy season and meditates on the meditation of compassion sees Brahmā; he converses with Brahmā, talks with Brahmā, and deliberates with Brahmā.
Sir, I wish to retreat into seclusion for the four months of the rainy season and to meditate on the meditation of compassion.
"He is not to be approached by anyone except for the purpose of offering him food.
"Then, let the venerable Govinda do as he deems fit.
Thereupon, sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those six kshatriyas; having approached them, he said this to the six kshatriyas:
“Sir, such a fine reputation has spread about me:
‘The brahmin Mahāgovinda can truly see Brahmā; the brahmin Mahāgovinda can truly converse with Brahmā, discuss with him, and deliberate with him.
Yet, sir, I do not see Brahmā, nor do I converse with Brahmā, nor discuss with Brahmā, nor deliberate with Brahmā.”
Moreover, I have heard this from aged and elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:

"Whoever retreats into seclusion for the four months of the rainy season and meditates on the meditation of compassion sees Brahmā, converses with Brahmā, talks with Brahmā, and deliberates with Brahmā.
Sir, I wish to retreat into seclusion for the four months of the rainy season and to meditate on the meditation of compassion.
“No one should approach me, except for one who brings food.
“Then, let the venerable Govinda do as he deems fit.
Then, sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda went to those seven wealthy brahmins and the seven hundred bath-graduates.
He approached them; having approached, he said this to those seven great brahmin householders and the seven hundred initiated bath-graduates:
"Gentlemen, such a fine reputation has spread concerning me:
'The brahmin Mahāgovinda can indeed see Brahmā; the brahmin Mahāgovinda can indeed converse with, speak with, and consult with Brahmā.'"
"However, sir, I do not see Brahmā, nor do I converse with Brahmā, nor speak with Brahmā, nor discuss with Brahmā.
But I have heard this from aged, elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:
'He who retreats into seclusion for the four months of the rains and meditates on the absorption of compassion sees Brahmā; he converses with Brahmā, speaks with Brahmā, and discusses with Brahmā.'"
"In that case, sirs, recite the mantras you have heard and mastered in detail, and teach the mantras to one another.
I wish, sirs, to retire into seclusion for the four months of the rains to meditate on the meditation of compassion;
I am not to be approached by anyone except for the bringing of a meal."
“Now, Master Govinda, you may do as you deem fit.
Then, sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached his forty wives of equal status; having approached them, he said this to his forty wives of equal status:
“Ladies, such a fine report concerning me has spread abroad:”
‘The brahmin Mahāgovinda has seen Brahmā; the brahmin Mahāgovinda converses with, speaks to, and deliberates with Brahmā.
But, lady, I have not seen Brahmā, nor do I converse with Brahmā, nor speak with Brahmā, nor deliberate with Brahmā.
However, I have heard this from aged and elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:
‘He who retreats into seclusion for the four months of the rains and meditates on the absorption of compassion sees Brahmā, converses with Brahmā, talks with Brahmā, and deliberates with Brahmā.
‘Lady, I wish to retreat into seclusion for the four months of the rains and to meditate on the absorption of compassion;
I am not to be approached by anyone except for the bringing of a single meal offering.’
“Now, sir, please do as you see fit.
Then, Master, the brahmin Mahāgovinda had a new assembly hall built to the east of the city and retired there for the four months of the rains retreat, absorbed in the meditation on compassion;
no one approached him except for the delivery of his daily meal.
Then, sir, at the end of four months, a sense of longing and anxiety arose in the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
"I have indeed heard this from aged, elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:

'Whoever retreats into seclusion for the four months of the rains and meditates on the meditation of compassion sees Brahmā; he converses with Brahmā, talks with Brahmā, and deliberates with Brahmā.'"
"Yet, sir, I do not see Brahmā; I do not converse with Brahmā, I do not talk with Brahmā, nor do I deliberate with Brahmā.
Then, sir, the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the brahmin Mahāgovinda—just as...
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
even so, vanishing from the Brahma-world, he appeared before the brahmin Mahāgovinda.
Then, sir, fear arose in the brahmin Mahāgovinda, trepidation arose, and his hair stood on end, as happens when one sees a form never seen before.
Then, sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda, terrified, agitated, and with his hair standing on end, addressed Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra in verse:
“O worthy one, who are you? You are handsome, renowned, and glorious.”
“Not knowing it, we ask you:
how shall we come to know it?
“They indeed know me as a youth.”
In the Brahma-world I am eternal;
all the gods know me thus— know it so, Govinda.”
“Seating, water, and foot-washing,
honey and vegetables— these are for Brahmā;
we ask you, sir, regarding these offerings.”
"May your honor accept our offering.
"We accept your offering,
O Govinda, just as you describe it."
For the sake of welfare and benefit in this very life,
and for happiness in the future world,
you have been granted leave; ask whatever you wish.
"Whatever has been desired.
Then, sir, it occurred to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
"I have been granted leave by Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra."
“What should I ask the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra—matters pertaining to this present life or matters pertaining to the future?
Then, sir, it occurred to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
“I am skilled in matters pertaining to this present life; others also ask me about matters pertaining to this present life.”
“What if I were now to ask Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra about matters pertaining to the future life?
Then, sir, the brahmin Mahāgovinda addressed Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra with a verse:
“I ask Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra:”
“Doubting, one understands the state free from doubt;
standing where, and training in what,
does a mortal attain the deathless world of Brahmā?”
“O Brahmā, having abandoned possessiveness among human beings,
become solitary and intent on compassion;
free from the stench of raw flesh and abstaining from sexual intercourse, [live thus].”
“Established here and training here,
a mortal attains the deathless Brahma-world.
“I understand, sir, that ‘having abandoned possessiveness’ refers to this.”
Here, someone, having abandoned a small mass of wealth or a large mass of wealth,
having abandoned a small circle of relatives or a large circle of relatives, shaves off his hair and beard,
puts on saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
"Thus, sir, I understand: 'having abandoned attachment.
And I understand, sir: 'become solitary.
Here, someone resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw."
"Thus, sir, I understand that one is 'become one.
I understand, sir, that one is 'devoted to compassion.
Here, someone dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by compassion, and likewise the second, and likewise..."

The third [direction], and likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, in every way, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Thus, sir, I understand you to mean that one is "devoted to compassion."
"But when you speak, venerable sir, I do not understand what the 'raw stench' among humans is, O Brahmā. Tell me here,
O wise one, for those who do not know."
“By what are people obstructed so that they go to states of deprivation, being shut out from the Brahma-world?
“Anger, lying, deceit, and dishonesty.”
Meanness, overweening pride, and envy;
longing, distraction, and malice toward others;
greed, hatred, conceit, and delusion.
“Those who are devoted to these things are foul-smelling,
bound for states of deprivation,
and shut out from the Brahma-world. “As I understand what you, sir, have said regarding these ‘raw-smells,’ they cannot be easily subdued by one living the household life.”
“Sir, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Then, Master Govinda, do as you deem it the right time.
6.4. The Addressing of King Reṇu.
Then, sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached King Reṇu; having approached him, he said this to King Reṇu:
"Your majesty, please seek another chaplain now who shall govern your kingdom.
I wish, sir, to go forth from the home life into homelessness."
"Indeed, as I have heard Brahmā speaking of the 'stench of the raw,' these [defilements] cannot be easily subdued by one living the household life.
Therefore, sirs, I shall go forth from the home into the homeless state.
"I address the King:"
"I shall serve King Reṇu;
you should know me as such by my kingship,
for I do not delight in the office of chaplain."
“If you are deficient in sensual pleasures,
I shall fulfill them for you;
whoever harms you, I shall restrain.”
I am the commander of the army,
and you are my father and I am your son;
O Govinda, do not abandon us!
“There is nothing lacking for me in sensual pleasures,
nor is there anyone who has harmed me;
having heard the words of a non-human being,”
"Therefore, I do not delight in the household life.
"What is the appearance of this non-human being?
What purpose did he speak to you?"
“Having heard what you have said, you have abandoned us in our home and become a perfected one. [The Buddha replied:
“In the past, when I had observed the fast...”
While I was desirous of performing a sacrifice,
a fire was kindled,
fanned by blades of kusa grass.
Then Brahmā Sanantana appeared to me from the Brahma-world;
he answered my question.
“Having heard that, I find no pleasure in the household life. “I believe you,
O Govinda, in what you say.”
Having heard the voice of a non-human being,
how could you speak otherwise?
We shall follow your lead.
"May the Master be our Govinda;
like a beryl gem,
free from flaws, stainless and beautiful."
"Thus shall we live pure,
following the instruction of Govinda.
If the venerable Govinda goes forth from the home life into homelessness, we too shall go forth from the home life into homelessness."
"Then whatever destination you have shall be our destination as well.
6.5. The Addressing of the Six Kshatriyas Then, sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those six kshatriyas; having approached them, he said this to the six kshatriyas:
“Now, sirs, seek another chaplain who shall rule over your kingdom.
I wish, gentlemen, to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
For according to what I have heard Brahmā speak regarding the ‘stench of raw flesh,’ those [impurities] cannot be easily suppressed while one dwells at home.”
“I shall go forth, sirs, from the home life into homelessness.
Then, sirs, those six kṣatriyas stepped aside and reflected thus:
“These brahmins are indeed greedy for wealth.”
"What if we were to win over the brahmin Mahāgovinda with wealth?
They approached the brahmin Mahāgovinda and said this:
"Sir, there is indeed abundant property in these seven kingdoms; from that, whatever amount you require may be brought to you."
“Enough, sir! This great wealth of mine is indeed due to you alone.
Having abandoned it all, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
For as I have heard Brahmā speaking of the ‘stench’ (āmagandha), these are not easily suppressed by one living at home.”
“I shall go forth, sirs, from the home life into homelessness.
Then, sirs, those six khattiyas, having stepped aside to one side, reflected thus:
“These brahmins are indeed greedy for women;”
"What if we were to win over the brahmin Mahāgovinda with women?
They approached the brahmin Mahāgovinda and said this:
"Sir, there are many women in these seven kingdoms; from among them, as many as you require may be brought to you."
“Enough, sir; I too have forty wives of equal status.
Having abandoned them all, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
For as I have heard Brahmā speaking of the ‘stench of raw flesh,’ these are not easy to subdue for one living the household life.”
“Sir, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“If Master Govinda goes forth from the home life into homelessness, we too shall go forth from the home life into homelessness; for whatever is your destination shall be our destination as well.
“If you abandon sensual pleasures...”
Wherever there is an ordinary person,
you must exert yourselves with firm resolve,
composed in the power of patience.
This is the path, the straight path;
this is the unsurpassed path;
the true Dhamma protected by the virtuous.
“...for rebirth in the Brahma-world.
“In that case, let Master Govinda wait for seven years.
At the end of seven years, we too shall go forth from the household life into homelessness; then whatever is your destination shall be our destination as well.”
“Seven years, sir, is indeed too long; I am not able, venerable sirs, to wait for seven years.
For who, sir, knows of the span of life? The world beyond must be traversed;
this is the time to reflect, to awaken, to do what is wholesome, and to lead the holy life. For one who is born, there is no escaping death.”
“Just as I have heard Brahmā speaking of the ‘stench of raw flesh,’ these [pleasures] cannot be easily subdued by one living the household life.
Therefore, sir, I shall go forth from the home into the homeless state.
“In that case, let Master Govinda wait for six years... [as before]... ”
May he wait for five years… may he wait for four years… may he wait for three years…
“Wait two years… wait one year;
at the end of one year we too shall go forth from the home life into homelessness, and then whatever is your destination shall be our destination.
“Sir, one year is indeed too long; I am not able to wait for one year.”
"Who indeed, sir, knows the span of life?
The world beyond must be traversed; this is the time for reflection, for awakening, for doing what is wholesome, and for living the holy life. For one who is born, there is no escaping death.
Now, according to what I have heard from Brahmā as he spoke of the 'stench of raw flesh,' these things are not easily mastered by one dwelling in a household."
“I shall go forth, sir, from the home life into homelessness.

“In that case, let Master Govinda wait for seven months; at the end of seven months we too shall go forth from the home life into homelessness. Then whatever is your destination shall be our destination as well.
“Seven months is indeed too long, sir; I am not able to wait for Master for seven months.”
"Who indeed, sir, knows the duration of life?
The next world must be traversed; this is the time for reflection, for awakening, for doing what is wholesome, and for living the holy life. For one who is born, there is no escaping death.
Now, according to what I have heard from Brahmā as he spoke of the 'stench of raw flesh,' these things are not easily subdued by one dwelling in a household."
"I shall go forth, sir, from the home life into homelessness.
"In that case, let Master Govinda wait for six months...
[or] let him wait for five months..."
May he wait for four months...
may he wait for three months...
may he wait for two months...
“May he wait for one month… may he wait for half a month;
at the end of half a month, we too shall go forth from the home life into homelessness, and whatever is his destination shall be our destination.
“Half a month is indeed too long, sir; I am not able to wait for half a month, venerable sirs.”
Who indeed, sir, knows the span of life?

The world beyond must be traversed; this is the time for reflection, for awakening, for doing what is wholesome, and for living the holy life (*brahmacariya*). For one who is born, there is no escaping death.
Now, according to what I have heard from Brahmā as he spoke of the "stench of raw flesh," these things are not easily subdued by one dwelling in a household.
“I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness, sir.
“In that case, let Master Govinda wait for seven days, until we have instructed our own sons and brothers in the kingdom;
at the end of seven days, we too shall go forth from the home life into homelessness. Then, whatever be your destination, [that shall be ours].”
“There will be no further rebirth.
“It will not be long, sir; I shall wait for seven days, sir, for seven days.
6.6. The Invitation of the Wealthy Brahmins and Others.
Then, sir, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those seven wealthy brahmins and seven hundred bath-graduates;
having approached them, he said this to those seven wealthy brahmins and seven hundred bath-graduates:
"Sirs, seek now another teacher who will teach you the mantras."
"I desire, sir, to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
For as I have heard Brahmā speaking of the 'stench of raw flesh,' those [defilements] are not easily subdued by one living at home;
therefore, sir, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness."
“May Master Govinda not go forth from the home life into homelessness. For,
sir, the life of a wanderer has little power and little gain,
whereas the status of a brahmin is of great power and great gain.”
“Sirs, do not speak thus: ‘The life of renunciation has little power and little gain, whereas the status of a brahmin has great power and great gain.
For who, sirs, is more powerful or has greater gain than I?
Indeed, sirs, at present I am like a king among kings, like Brahmā among brahmins, and like a deity among householders.”
"Having abandoned all that, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
For as I have heard Brahmā speaking of the 'stench of raw flesh,' those [defilements] are not easily subdued by one living at home.
Sir, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness."
“If Master Govinda goes forth from the home life into homelessness, we too shall go forth from the home life into homelessness; whatever be your destination, that shall be our destination.
Then, sirs, the Great Steward Brahmin approached his forty wives of equal status; having approached them, he said this to his forty wives of equal status:
“Whatever you desire, ladies, you may go to your own families or seek another husband.
As for me, ladies, I wish to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
For according to what I have heard Brahmā speaking of the ‘stench of raw flesh,’ those [impurities] are not easily suppressed by one living at home.”
“Lady, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“You are our kinsman for us who desire kin; you are our husband for us who desire a husband.
If Master Govinda goes forth from the home life into homelessness, we too shall go forth from the home life into homelessness. Whatever is your destination shall be our destination as well.”

6.8. The Great Steward’s Going-forth Then, sir, at the end of those seven days, the brahmin Mahāgovinda shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
And when the brahmin Mahāgovinda had gone forth, the seven anointed kṣatriya kings also [went forth].
And the great brahmin, seven hundred bath-graduates, forty wives of equal status,
many thousands of kshatriyas, many thousands of brahmins, many thousands of householders, and the women of the harem—
having shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron robes— [followed] Mahāgovinda.
They followed the Brahmin Mahāgovinda when he went forth from the home life into homelessness.
Surrounded by that assembly, O sir, the Brahmin Mahāgovinda wandered on tour through villages, market towns, and royal capitals.
And whenever, O sir, the Brahmin Mahāgovinda approached a village or a market town, there he was like a king among kings, like Brahmā among Brahmins, and like a deity among householders.
Now at that time, people stumbled or tripped, and they said:
"Homage to the brahmin Mahāgovinda! Homage to the sevenfold domestic priest!"
The brahmin Mahāgovinda, friends, dwelt having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;

likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity.
He dwelt pervading [the world] with a mind imbued with non-affliction. With a mind accompanied by compassion...
[and so on] ...with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy... [and so on].
With a mind accompanied by equanimity... [and so on] ...he dwelt pervading [the world] with a heart free from ill will.
And he taught the path to his disciples for companionship in the Brahma-world.
Now, sir, those who at that time were disciples of the brahmin Mahāgovinda understood the entire teaching in its entirety.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they were reborn in a happy destination, the Brahma-world.

Those who did not understand the teaching in its entirety, with some having been reborn in companionship with the Paranimmitavasavatti devas and others having been reborn in companionship with the Nimmānarati devas, with the breakup of the body, after death, attained such states.
Some were reborn in the company of the Tusita devas;
some were reborn in the company of the Yāma devas;
some were reborn in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Some were reborn in companionship with the gods of the Four Great Kings;
those who had fulfilled the very lowest grade of existence were reborn in the company of the gandhabbas.
Thus, sir, for all those sons of good family, the going forth was not in vain, it was not barren, but fruitful and productive.’”
“Does the Blessed One remember that?
“I do remember it, Pañcasikha.
At that time, I was the brahmin Mahāgovinda.”
I taught those disciples the path for companionship with the Brahma-world.

But that holy life of mine, Pañcasikha, did not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to awakening, nor to Nibbāna; it led only as far as rebirth in the Brahma-world.
However, this holy life of mine, Pañcasikha, leads exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.
And what, Pañcasikha, is that holy life which leads to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path.
That is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
"This, Pañcasikha, is that holy life which leads to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
But as for those disciples of mine, Pañcasikha, who understand the entire teaching in its entirety, they, through the destruction of the taints,
dwell having realized for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it and remained therein."

Those who do not understand the teaching in its entirety become, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, beings of spontaneous birth who attain final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world.

Those who do not understand the teaching in its entirety, some—through the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion—become once-returners; having returned to this world only once more, they will make an end of suffering.

"Those who do not understand the teaching in its entirety, some—through the complete destruction of three fetters—become stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment.
Thus, Pañcasikha, for all these sons of good family, the going forth is not in vain, it is fruitful, productive, and brings great results.
This is what the Blessed One said.

Pleased, Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabbas, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him with his right side toward him, and vanished right there.
The Mahāgovinda Sutta, the sixth, is finished.
